state.case_summary:
A 47-year-old man was referred for mechanical circulatory support for severe cardiogenic shock with multiorgan failure of unknown cause. One day earlier, he had undergone excision of a benign thyroglossal duct cyst, during which he experienced recurrent hypertensive episodes. After extubation, he developed profound hypotension and pulmonary oedema. Transthoracic echocardiography showed severely impaired left ventricular (LV) systolic function. Coronary angiography revealed no evidence of relevant coronary artery disease, and toxicological screening was negative. His medical history included chronic polyarthritis and treated arterial hypertension.

On transfer, he was invasively ventilated (PaO2/FiO2 30 mmHg), receiving norepinephrine at 2.5 µg/kg/min. Blood pressure was 75/49 mmHg, heart rate 180 b.p.m., with bilateral rales and basal dullness on chest percussion. He experienced pulseless electrical activity requiring 5 minutes of resuscitation. Bedside echocardiography demonstrated akinesia of all basal and mid LV segments with preserved apical contraction (left ventricular ejection fraction, 15%); right ventricular function was preserved (TAPSE 17 mm). On the basis of these findings, reverse takotsubo cardiomyopathy was suspected. A percutaneous LV assist device (Impella CP®) was implanted immediately. Endomyocardial biopsy revealed moderate chronically active myocarditis with diffuse interstitial remodelling, and PCR testing showed no evidence of acute or persistent myocardial infection.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

Options:
A. Pheochromocytoma
B. — “because of the typical LV kinetics, a reverse TTC was suspected
C. on imaging
D. Reverse TTC suspected
E. Coronary artery disease excluded
F. Toxic etiology excluded
G. Dilated cardiomyopathy considered but disfavored due to regional wall‐motion pattern
H. Acute myocarditis excluded by biopsy and PCR
